name: Dead Orchard to Darce Switch
description: A Darce needs an arm threaded through the armpit and around the neck; a Dead Orchard high leg triangle does not already contain that arm enclosure.
summary: A Darce needs an arm threaded through the armpit and around the neck; a Dead Orchard high leg triangle does not already contain that arm enclosure.
overview:
The initial Dead Orchard Control configuration must be identified before considering Darce Control. The defining feature is both shoulders and arms enclosed by the legs. An anaconda instead uses an arm loop around the neck and one arm from a front headlock; the two controls require different body configurations. The reviewed instruction does not establish a direct Dead Orchard Control-to-Darce Control connection. Release the original lock safely and establish the destination's own prerequisites; do not treat these checkpoints as a demonstrated continuous entry.

The legs form a high figure-four around the shoulder line, with both opposing arms inside. Both arms may be trapped, so agree on verbal and foot taps. Never stack the neck, wrench a knee into the leg triangle, or test a captured elbow by pulling hard. Open the original connection before either partner turns, rises or changes the captured limb.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Nathan Orchard — Dead Orchard, part 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XoiB1D2WJwE); [Ben Eddy — the Zombie pummel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JzSxFvNA5Uo).

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): What contains the arms at the starting checkpoint?
flashcards.answer: Dead Orchard encloses both opposing arms with the legs at the shoulder line.

plausible: High triangle with one arm outside
High shins without leg closure

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): Both hands are trapped in the initial control; how can they tap?
flashcards.answer: Agree on verbal and foot taps before drilling the both-arm capture, and release immediately on either signal.
flashcards.answer_line: An agreed verbal signal or foot tap

plausible: Free a hand before any stop signal
Tap mat with a still-trapped hand
trap: Wait for grip slack before signaling

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): What opens before changing from the high guard to a headlock?
flashcards.answer: Release the old leg enclosure and arm loading before seeking the separate head-and-arm position.

plausible: Only the hand supporting the shin
Only one foot; keep wrist tension
trap: Only wrist grip; leg triangle locked

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): Which separate position permits the new arm thread?
flashcards.answer: A Darce needs its own front or side head-and-arm relationship after the high guard ends; no direct switch is established.
flashcards.answer_line: Front/side access to neck and armpit

plausible: Facing guard with both arms in legs
Side access, head beyond arm reach

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): Which direction does the Darce arm travel?
flashcards.answer: The Darce thread enters at the armpit and travels around the neck before connecting to the supporting arm.

plausible: Under neck, then out toward armpit
Outside upper arm, then around neck

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): How is the new enclosure checked in a capture drill?
flashcards.answer: Check the new head-and-arm enclosure with the neck aligned and no finishing squeeze.

plausible: Grip joined with head turned away
Neck aligned with finishing squeeze

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce: which player and enclosure define the starting control?
flashcards.answer: The initial attack belongs to the bottom high-guard player, regardless of misleading retained graph seat labels.
flashcards.answer_line: Bottom player; both arms in leg trap

plausible: Top player inside the high guard
Bottom player; only one arm enclosed

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): What replaces the starting both-arm leg triangle?
flashcards.answer: These are different configurations: a both-arm leg trap and a separately established head-and-one-arm choke.
flashcards.answer_line: Arm loop around head and one arm

plausible: Arm loop around head and both arms
Leg triangle with one arm outside
trap: Arm loop around only the neck

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (attacker): An elbow stays caught when the body turns; what first?
flashcards.answer: A fixed elbow must be released before either partner changes orientation; a route label does not justify turning through the trap.
flashcards.answer_line: Release the elbow before the turn

plausible: Keep wrist fixed; rotate the torso
Tighten old triangle to guide turn
trap: Open one leg; keep pulling the wrist

defender.description: Dead Orchard to Darce Switch (defender): An arm passing beneath the neck toward the armpit signals the Anaconda enclosure. Preserve space between the shoulder and neck before the attacker closes the arm loop.
defender.overview:
The initial Dead Orchard Control configuration must be identified before considering Darce Control. The defining feature is both shoulders and arms enclosed by the legs. An anaconda instead uses an arm loop around the neck and one arm from a front headlock; the two controls require different body configurations. The reviewed instruction does not establish a direct Dead Orchard Control-to-Darce Control connection. Release the original lock safely and establish the destination's own prerequisites; do not treat these checkpoints as a demonstrated continuous entry.

An arm passing beneath the neck toward the armpit signals the Anaconda enclosure. Preserve space between the shoulder and neck before the attacker closes the arm loop. Do not fight a secured loop by twisting the neck or planting the head against a roll.

Hand fight before the enclosure becomes tight, while keeping the trapped elbow connected to the torso. Stop if the neck enclosure is secure rather than relying on a last-second roll. Recover posture and guard or turtle only when the head and shoulder can move freely.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Protect the neck as the new arm thread approaches, and make an early escape by keeping the trapped shoulder from closing the neck space. A framed hip escape can recover knee space after the head and arm are free; it must not twist through a secured Darce.

Tap before symptoms: Stop if the neck enclosure is secure rather than relying on a last-second roll.
Rebuild base after release: Recover posture and guard or turtle only when the head and shoulder can move freely.

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (defender): Which incoming arm path signals the new Darce threat?
flashcards.answer: Recognize the armpit-to-neck Darce thread. The old card's Anaconda description does not identify the intended new choke.

plausible: Under neck toward the far armpit
Outside upper arm around the neck

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (defender): What space matters before the new arm loop closes?
flashcards.answer: Preserve shoulder-to-neck space early before the Darce arm loop brings them together.

plausible: Gap outside the captured elbow
Gap under the opposite free armpit
trap: Only a gap between chin and chest

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (defender): How should your head stay during early grip defense?
flashcards.answer: Maintain head alignment; do not resist a secured loop by twisting or planting the head.
flashcards.answer_line: Head aligned with torso in the loop

plausible: Head turned with shoulder held fixed
Forehead braced while torso moves
trap: Chin lifted with chest still folded

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (defender): When does hand fighting have its best preventive window?
flashcards.answer: Address the approaching grip before the neck loop tightens, keeping the trapped arm compact.
flashcards.answer_line: Before a tight supporting grip joins

plausible: After tight grip closes neck space
Only after a roll tightens the loop
trap: After head stops moving in the grip

flashcards.question: Dead Orchard to Darce (defender): The neck loop is secured; what response precedes recovery?
flashcards.answer: Once the choke is secure, tap. Guard recovery belongs after the head and arm are released.

plausible: Peel grip with neck still enclosed
Lift chin before support arm unlocks
trap: Wait for a roll to open the arm loop
